hero.association: Aruban Football Federation / Arubaanse Voetbal Bond (AVB)

sections.title: Country
sections.subtitle: A small Dutch Caribbean country just off Venezuela

paragraphs: Only 25 km north of Venezuela, Aruba is a 180-km² Caribbean island and an autonomous constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands. Around 110,000 people live there; Dutch and Papiamento are official languages, with Spanish and English also widespread.

sections.title: Recent history
sections.subtitle: Caquetío roots, Dutch rule, oil and Status Aparte

entries.heading: Caquetío Aruba and Spanish rule
paragraphs: Aruba’s first known inhabitants were Caquetío Arawaks with close links to today’s Venezuela. Spain claimed the island after Alonso de Ojeda’s 1499 voyage; many Caquetíos were deported in 1514, although some were later returned from the mainland.

entries.heading: Dutch rule and the old island economy
paragraphs: The Dutch West India Company seized Aruba from Spain in 1636. Apart from British occupation during the Napoleonic Wars, Dutch rule endured. Gold, phosphate and aloe shaped the 19th-century economy.

entries.heading: Oil transforms Aruba
paragraphs: Lago Oil opened in 1924 to refine Venezuelan crude and turned Aruba into an industrial hub. During World War II the refinery was strategically important to Allied aviation fuel and was attacked by a German submarine in 1942. Tourism later grew as oil employment declined.

entries.heading: Status Aparte
paragraphs: Aruba became part of the autonomous Netherlands Antilles in 1954. A long movement for separation culminated on 1 January 1986, when Status Aparte made Aruba a country of its own within the Kingdom. A planned route to full independence was dropped in 1994.

sections.title: Football origins
sections.subtitle: A catalogue ball, oil-company football and the rise of Aruba’s great clubs

entries.heading: Gerard de Veer’s football
paragraphs: Aruban football begins with a catalogue. In 1909 businessman Gerard de Veer saw a football advertised and ordered one for his sons Eddy and Geffy. That year pastor Gerrit Eybers and the De Veer brothers formed Aruba Voetbal Vereniging, the island’s first club.

The pioneers cleared a cactus-covered plot in Oranjestad and initially split AVV into red and blue sides because there was nobody else to play. Dutch teaching brothers later introduced football in schools.

entries.heading: The first championship
paragraphs: Around 1920/21 an early football association appeared, although even the AVB no longer knows its name or officials. It organised Aruba’s first recorded championship in 1921, won by Wilhelmina.
Vitesse, founded the next year, became one of the 1920s’ most popular clubs. Aruba’s first recorded inter-island club match came in 1924 when Sparta of Curaçao visited Vitesse.

entries.heading: Oil spreads the game
paragraphs: Lago and other oil companies transformed the island. Workers, money and new settlements carried football beyond Oranjestad to Savaneta, Santa Cruz and Noord.

In April 1930 an Aruba selection travelled to Curaçao. A new Arubaanse Voetbal Bond formed that October under Dr Jacobo ‘Coco’ Arends. To secure land for its own sports park, the AVB was formally constituted on 29 January 1932—the date it uses today.

entries.heading: Hollandia, Lago and an uncertain first AVB champion
paragraphs: Several clubs appeared during the 1920s, including Hollandia in Oranjestad in 1923 and Lago FC, created by oil-company exploration workers around 1929.
The first AVB champion remains uncertain in the source: the federation’s own account names Hollandia, while contemporary press mentions Lago for 1930/31.

entries.heading: Wilhelmina Sport Park and Aruba Juniors
paragraphs: Wilhelmina Sport Park opened in 1933 with two visits from the Curaçao selection. Aruba Juniors became the first Aruban club to tour Curaçao, while sides from Bonaire, Suriname, Venezuela and Colombia visited Aruba during the decade.
SV Aruba Juniors had been founded in Socotoro on 5 February 1932 by neighbourhood friends led by Selin Fingal, who proposed the name after reading about Argentinos Juniors and Boca Juniors.

entries.heading: RCA — the first dynasty
paragraphs: Racing Club Aruba was founded in Solito/Oranjestad in 1934 from a team organised the year before by Emirto Reinhardt. It was first formally called A.B.C.—Aruba’s Beste Club.
The club adopted RCA in 1937. From 1938 to 1960 it won every championship except five: four went to Aruba Juniors and one to Hollandia.

entries.heading: NAVB, NAVU and the Kopa Antiano
paragraphs: Aruba and Curaçao created the N.A.V.B. in 1941, but the experiment ended in 1946. After the Netherlands Antilles were formed politically, the N.A.V.U. followed in 1958 and the first Kopa Antiano was staged in 1960.
Aruban clubs won only two editions. RCA became champions in 1965 after two dramatic matches against Scherpenheuvel; in 1970 Dakota and Estrella finished level at the top.

entries.heading: Dakota and Estrella
paragraphs: SV Dakota, founded in the Oranjestad neighbourhood of Dakota in 1947, became RCA’s great domestic rival and won its first championship in 1961.

Estrella was born in Santa Cruz in 1948 as the football arm of the Catholic Sint Jozefbond youth association. From the 1960s through the 1970s, RCA, Dakota and Estrella shared almost all the major domestic honours.

entries.heading: Status Aparte gives Aruba its own FIFA identity
paragraphs: Status Aparte changed the football map. Aruba left the Netherlands Antilles in 1986 and gained its own international identity; the AVB entered FIFA in 1988. From then on Aruban clubs competed solely for the Aruban championship and the national team could enter FIFA competitions.

entries.heading: The LIPROF breakaway
paragraphs: RCA, La Fama, Bubali, Dakota and San Luis broke away into the dissident semi-professional LIPROF in 1990 over complaints against the AVB. RCA won the one-season competition, but the title is not official.
The split nevertheless altered the island’s football landscape. With traditional powers missing, the AVB promoted lower-division sides and two eventually became champions.

entries.heading: Riverplate and Deportivo Nacional
paragraphs: Riverplate, founded in Madiki in 1953 and inspired by its Argentine namesake, won the Aruban title in 1993. Deportivo Nacional, born in Palm Beach in 1970, later completed its rise from the lower ranks by becoming champion in 2000.

entries.heading: Britannia becomes a modern power
paragraphs: SV Britannia, founded in Piedra Plat in 1957, reached the top flight only in 2001 but quickly became a major force. The source credits the club with seven league titles.

In 2018, Deportivo Nacional became the first Aruban club to progress beyond the group stage of the CFU Club Shield and, in the source, remains the only Aruban side ever to advance beyond the first round of a Caribbean or continental club competition.
COVID hit tourism-dependent Aruba hard and the 2019/20 league was abandoned. The competition returned in reduced form in 2020/21.
Britannia entered the source’s present day on a three-year championship streak, with Dakota and RCA still their principal challengers.

sections.title: Major competitions
sections.subtitle: Gold League, Silver League, Calle 4 and the Caribbean route

cards.title: Division di Honor
cards.text: Clubs first play a single nine-match round. The top six advance to the Gold League; the bottom four enter the Silver League promotion/relegation phase.

cards.title: Gold League → Calle 4 → Final
cards.text: The six Gold League clubs play a double round robin. The top four move into Calle 4, another three-match round robin, and the top two meet in the Championship Final. Britannia beat Sporting 3–1 in the source’s 2026 final.

cards.title: Silver League
cards.text: The bottom four Honor Division clubs mix with Division Uno sides in two groups. Group winners stay in or are promoted to the top flight, while playoff winners take the remaining Honor places.

cards.title: Copa Betico Croes
cards.text: All Division di Honor clubs and the best six from Division Uno take part. Britannia lead the source’s roll of honour with eight wins; Dakota beat La Fama 4–2 in the 2026 final.

cards.title: CFU Club Shield
cards.text: Aruba’s league champions enter the CFU Club Shield. Its finalists qualify for the professional Caribbean Cup.

cards.title: Caribbean Cup → Champions Cup
cards.text: The Caribbean Cup sends its top three into the CONCACAF Champions Cup. No Aruban club has completed that full route since the Shield was introduced in 2018.

sections.title: Main clubs
sections.subtitle: RCA, Dakota, Estrella and a modern Britannia dynasty

cards.title: Racing Club Aruba
cards.meta: Record 33 league titles in the source
cards.text: RCA are Aruba’s historic giant. Founded in 1934, they dominated the early AVB era and became the island’s first Kopa Antiano champions in 1965.

cards.title: Dakota & Estrella
cards.text: Dakota have 17 league titles in the source and dominated much of the 1960s–80s. Santa Cruz’s Estrella have 12 and supplied Aruba’s other Antillean championship in 1970.

cards.title: Britannia
cards.text: The Piedra Plat club won its first league in 2004/05 and has seven in the source, including the 2024–26 three-peat. Britannia also lead the Copa Betico Croes roll of honour.

cards.title: Nacional, Bubali, La Fama & Riverplate
cards.text: Noord’s Deportivo Nacional and Bubali, Savaneta’s La Fama and Madiki’s Riverplate complete much of Aruba’s modern historic club landscape.

sections.title: National team
sections.subtitle: From island selection to an independent FIFA team

entries.heading: Two lives
paragraphs: Aruba’s national-team history has two lives. An island selection existed from 1930, but internationally Aruba largely belonged to the Netherlands Antilles. Only after Status Aparte and FIFA admission in 1988 did today’s FIFA national team fully emerge.

entries.heading: The first island selection
paragraphs: The first Aruba selection travelled to Curaçao in April 1930. Trips to Curaçao, Suriname and Trinidad followed. The rivalry with Curaçao gradually became competitive, with first draws in 1937 and, according to the AVB, Aruba’s first victory in 1944.

entries.heading: Arubans in the Netherlands Antilles Olympic team
paragraphs: Seven Arubans made the Helsinki Olympic squad. Briezen, Brion and Brokke started against Türkiye, and Juan Briezen scored in the 82nd minute. It remains Aruba’s only Olympic football appearance.

entries.heading: Aruba at the CCCF Championship
paragraphs: Aruba entered separately in the 1955 CCCF Championship, beating Cuba 5–1 and drawing Honduras 1–1. Fifth place remains the island’s best CCCF finish.

entries.heading: The Antillean golden generation
paragraphs: Aruba then fed fully into the Netherlands Antilles. With a strong Aruban presence, the 1960 CCCF side finished level with Costa Rica before losing a playoff, and the 1961 team finished third.

The Netherlands Antilles swept the 1962 Central American and Caribbean Games, then took bronze at the inaugural 1963 CONCACAF Championship and again in 1969. The latter was the swan song of the generation, with Aruban representation already declining.

entries.heading: An independent national team returns
paragraphs: Status Aparte revived Aruba’s independent national team. After FIFA admission, the 1989 Caribbean Championship campaign was brutal: Trinidad & Tobago won 11–0, still the heaviest recorded defeat in the source. A 0–0 draw with Grenada delivered the first FIFA-era point.

entries.heading: The difficult early 1990s
paragraphs: Aruba did not win a match in the 1990, 1991 or 1992 Caribbean Cup qualifiers and skipped 1993 and 1994. In 1995 two vibrant ties against the old Netherlands Antilles rivals ended in a 7–5 aggregate defeat.

entries.heading: First World Cup qualifying campaign
paragraphs: Aruba entered World Cup qualifying for the first time in 1996 and lost both legs to the Dominican Republic.

In 1997 Caribbean Cup qualifying, Aruba beat the Netherlands Antilles 2–1 before Jamaica stopped them in the second phase. In 1998 they beat French Guiana and drew Suriname 3–3, but another defeat to the Netherlands Antilles ended the campaign.

entries.heading: First World Cup qualifying victory
paragraphs: Aruba beat Puerto Rico 4–2 at home and drew 2–2 away to advance 6–4 on aggregate—their first World Cup qualifying tie victory. Barbados ended the run in the next round.

entries.heading: A difficult decade and a wider diaspora
paragraphs: The next decade brought heavy qualifying defeats, but Aruba gradually became more connected to its Dutch diaspora, widening the available player pool.

entries.heading: Record win at home
paragraphs: Hosting preliminary Caribbean Cup qualifying, Aruba beat Turks & Caicos Islands 1–0 and British Virgin Islands 7–0—the record victory in the source—but a 2–0 loss to French Guiana prevented progression.

entries.heading: The strange Barbados disqualification
paragraphs: Barbados won both legs against Aruba but fielded suspended Hadan Holligan in the second. FIFA awarded Aruba a 3–0 victory, turning a 3–0 aggregate defeat into a 3–2 passage.
Saint Vincent & the Grenadines then won the next tie 3–2 on aggregate despite two Erixon Danso goals in Oranjestad.

entries.heading: Nations League begins
paragraphs: Aruba took the final League B place in 2019–20 qualifying but then lost every group match against Jamaica, Guyana and Antigua & Barbuda and fell to League C.

In 2022/23 they beat Saint Martin but Saint Kitts & Nevis took promotion. The 2023/24 campaign was completely different: Aruba won all four matches against Cayman Islands and US Virgin Islands and returned to League B.

entries.heading: Qatar 2022 qualifying
paragraphs: Aruba lost heavily to Suriname and Bermuda, beat Cayman Islands 3–1 and then lost 7–0 to Canada. Three points left them fourth in the group.

entries.heading: League B proves too difficult
paragraphs: Aruba went winless against Haiti, Puerto Rico and Sint Maarten in 2024/25. A 5–1 defeat to Puerto Rico mathematically relegated them, and Aruba returned to League C for 2026/27.

entries.heading: 2026 World Cup qualifying
paragraphs: The World Cup road ended in Round Two. Aruba lost to Curaçao, surrendered a 2–0 lead against Saint Lucia, drew Barbados and lost heavily to Haiti. Two points left them well short of the two group leaders.

entries.heading: FIFA Series champions
paragraphs: An unexpected breakthrough followed at the FIFA Series Rwanda B. Aruba beat Macau 4–1 and Liechtenstein 4–1 to win the section. The source describes FIFA as calling it the most prestigious title in the national team’s history. Jaybriën Romano scored three goals and won Player of the Series.

entries.heading: The next Nations League challenge
paragraphs: Aruba enter League C, Group B with Antigua & Barbuda and Anguilla. Group winners plus the best runner-up advance to the new League C Championship and earn promotion to League B.

sections.title: Historical line-up
sections.subtitle: An XI spanning the pre-FIFA, Netherlands Antilles and modern eras
sections.intro: Comparing the old island selections, Arubans who represented the Netherlands Antilles and the modern FIFA national team is unusually difficult, so the source deliberately spans all three eras.

players.name: Eric Abdul
players.description: A long-serving goalkeeper developed in Sparta Rotterdam’s youth system who guarded Aruba through three World Cup cycles.

players.name: Theric Ruiz
players.description: A durable defender across more than a decade and nine World Cup qualifying appearances.

players.name: Nickenson Paul
players.description: The modern caps record holder in the source and a mainstay of Aruba’s back line.

players.name: François Croes
players.description: A centre-back with more than 20 international caps who also played locally for SV Estrella.

players.name: Leroy Oehlers
players.description: A Dutch-born Aruba left-back who earned around 20 caps.

players.name: Gregor Breinburg
players.description: The island’s most accomplished modern club professional, with long spells at De Graafschap, NEC, Sparta and ADO.

players.name: Erik Santos de Gouveia
players.description: A consistent midfield presence for a decade, with 20+ caps and international goals.

players.name: Walter Bennett
players.description: A modern attacking midfielder with 30+ caps in the source.

players.name: Joshua John
players.description: One of the highest-level club players to represent Aruba, with experience at Sparta Rotterdam and Nordsjælland among others.

players.name: Terence Groothusen
players.description: Six international goals in the source and a long-running reference point in attack.

players.name: Juan Briezen
players.description: Aruba’s Olympic goalscorer with the Netherlands Antilles at Helsinki 1952.

sections.closing: Jorge Brion, Ricardo Helder, Lucas Hernandez, Leo Rodriguez, Matthew Lentink, Ronald Gómez, Benjamin Maria, Diederick Luydens and current captain Bradley Martis are among the omissions.

recordGroups.title: Team records
items: First island selection: v Curaçao, April 1930.
First FIFA-era point: 0–0 v Grenada, 21 May 1989.
Biggest win: 7–0 v British Virgin Islands, 1 June 2014.
Heaviest recorded defeat: Trinidad & Tobago 11–0 Aruba, 23 April 1989.
Best FIFA ranking in the source: 112th.

sections.title: Notable stadiums
sections.subtitle: The national stadium and three unmistakably local grounds

cards.title: Compleho Deportivo Guillermo Prospero Trinidad
cards.text: The national ground opened in April 1952 as Wilhelmina Stadion, replacing the old Wilhelmina Sport Park. After major redevelopment it reopened in 1994 under its present name and remains Aruba’s main international venue.

cards.title: Compleho Deportivo Frans Figaroa
cards.text: Aruba’s principal alternative football venue. It honours Frans Figaroa, former AVB chairman, Netherlands Antilles Olympic Committee head and Aruban political leader. Several Division di Honor clubs use the ground.

cards.title: Compleho Deportivo Franklyn Bareño
cards.text: A distinctive community ground with Aruba’s Hooiberg rising behind it. The complex is the home of modern powerhouse SV Britannia.

cards.title: SV La Fama home ground
cards.text: A modest, unmistakably local football ground with a small covered stand and the club’s name painted across its facilities—a neighbourhood home in southern Aruba.

entries.heading: Aruba remains in the race
paragraphs: CONCACAF qualifying begins in September 2027. Aruba remains eligible for the 2030 FIFA World Cup qualification process.
